analysis.one_liner: Caps the size and leverage of the nation's largest banks to make them safer.
analysis.headline: The bill to cap big-bank size and leverage was sent to the House Financial Services Committee and two of its subcommittees and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would limit how big and how leveraged the largest U.S. banks can be. It would bar any bank holding company from holding more than 10% of the nation's deposits, bar any financial company from holding more than 10% of all financial-company liabilities, require the biggest banks and large nonbank financial companies to hold tangible common equity equal to at least 10% of their average total assets (counting off-balance-sheet assets), and cap nondeposit liabilities at roughly 2-3% of U.S. GDP. Regulators would be required to make companies that exceed the limits sell assets or raise capital to comply [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary depositors and taxpayers, because banks forced to hold more of their own money and shed off-balance-sheet risks are less likely to fail in ways that trigger bailouts or freezes on household access to credit and deposits. Smaller banks also gain a fairer chance to compete when giant banks cannot dominate national deposits [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Bars any bank holding company from holding more than 10% of all U.S. insured deposits and requires the Federal Reserve to force any bank over the limit to sell deposit liabilities to unaffiliated firms [S2] [S3].

Requires every bank holding company with $50 billion or more in assets, and every Federal Reserve-supervised nonbank financial company, to maintain tangible common equity of at least 10% of average total consolidated assets, with off-balance-sheet assets counted in the total [S2] [S3].

Counts off-balance-sheet assets, including financings of assets where the issuer retains more than minimal economic or reputational risk, in both the leverage and liability calculations, closing a route banks used to hide risk before the 2008 crisis [S3].

Caps a bank holding company's nondeposit liabilities at 2% of U.S. GDP and a nonbank financial company's at 3%, and directs the Federal Reserve to use prompt corrective action—requiring capital raises, asset sales, or activity limits—for violators [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The largest bank holding companies and big nonbank financial companies would bear the cost: they would have to raise large amounts of new capital, sell assets and deposit liabilities, or break up operations to fit under the size, concentration, and leverage caps, which would compress their returns and constrain growth.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wall Street's largest banks and financial firms

drawbacks.text: The 10% tangible common equity requirement is far stricter than the capital standards banks and international regulators operated under, and institutions with $50 billion or more in assets would have had to comply within one year of enactment, which critics argued could force abrupt asset sales and shrink the supply of credit [S3].

The bill leaves substantial discretion to the Federal Reserve: it lets the Board set separate liability limits for insurance companies and exclude foreign deposits from the nondeposit-liability calculation, so the real bite of the caps would depend on regulator choices [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: a banking system whose giant firms are smaller, less indebted, and less able to hide risks off the balance sheet, at the cost of lower returns for large bank shareholders and possibly some reduction in big-bank lending capacity. The strict one-year compliance timeline for existing violators and the regulator discretion built into the limits were real design weaknesses, but the underlying goal—making bank failures less catastrophic for depositors and taxpayers—was squarely a public-protection measure.

outcome.mechanism: The House Financial Services Committee never took the bill up; it sat with the committee, then was referred to two of its subcommittees in October 2012, and the 112th Congress ended in January 2013 without any markup or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Miller of North Carolina introduced the bill on May 10, 2012, joined by Rep. Keith Ellison as an original cosponsor [S3].
The House referred the bill to the Committee on Financial Services the day it was introduced; no further committee action, markup, or floor vote ever occurred [S5].

On October 1, 2012, the bill was referred to two subcommittees—Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, and Insurance, Housing and Community Opportunity—where it remained until the Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5].
The bill never gained broad support: only three House members cosponsored it, all Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest bank holding companies and Federal Reserve-supervised nonbank financial companies, which kept their existing size, leverage, and off-balance-sheet structures because the bill never advanced. Community banks and depositors gained nothing because the size caps were never put in place.

industries.note: The bill would force them under a 10% deposit share cap, a 10% liabilities cap, a 10% leverage ratio, and nondeposit-liability caps set off GDP, requiring massive capital raises or breakups. Their interest in blocking it ran against ordinary people's stake in a banking system less prone to crisis and bailouts.

industries.industry: Large nonbank financial companies (e.g., insurers and finance companies supervised by the Fed)
industries.note: They would face a 10% leverage requirement and a 3%-of-GDP nondeposit liability cap, though the bill lets the Board set separate limits for insurance companies and exclude foreign deposits, softening the impact.
Caps on the largest firms' deposit share and liabilities would keep giant competitors from dominating national deposits, improving their competitive position.
